No. 25A1096
In the Supreme Court of the United States 
___________________________________
SAMUEL RONAN, ET AL.
Applicants,
v. 
FRANK LAROSE, OHIO SECRETARY OF STATE, ET AL.
Respondents.
_______________________________________________________
ON APPLICATION FOR AN INJUNCTION PENDING APPEAL TO THE UNITED 
STATES COURT OF APPEALS FOR THE SIXTH CIRCUIT
_____________________________________________________
RESPONDENT’S RESPONSE IN OPPOSITION TO EMERGENCY 
APPLICATION FOR PRELIMINARY INJUNCTION PENDING APPEAL, 
ADMINISTRATIVE STAY, AND EXPEDITED BRIEFING
_______________________________________________________
DAVE YOST
Attorney General of Ohio
MATHURA J. SRIDHARAN*
Ohio Solicitor General
 *Counsel of Record
LAYNE H. TIESZEN
Deputy Solicitor General
30 E. Broad St., 17th Floor
Columbus, OH 43215
614.466.8980
Mathura.Sridharan@OhioAGO.gov
Counsel for Respondent
 Frank LaRose

1
INTRODUCTION
Samuel Ronan wanted to run for office in Ohio’s Republican primary as a Republican. Just one problem: he is a Democrat. At least that is what he has said—more 
than once. In fact, Ronan had spent over a decade on a mission: for “Democrats” to 
“primary Republicans in deep red districts, as Republicans.” App.217. And his campaign manager, Ana Cordero, confirmed that even in the upcoming Midterm Elections, their intent was to “torpedo the republican party from within.” App.361, 411–
12. He was ultimately removed from the May 2026 primary ballot for lying on his 
candidacy form about his membership in the Republican Party and willingness to 
abide by the Party’s principles, in contravention of Ohio’s good-faith candidacy-declaration requirement. Ohio Rev. Code §3513.07. 
Ronan (and Cordero) filed suit alleging violations of his First Amendment rights, 
the Elections Clause, and his due-process rights. After being twice refused by the 
lower courts, first for a preliminary injunction from the district court and next for an 
injunction pending appeal from the Sixth Circuit, Ronan now asks this Court for an 
extraordinary, first-in-time injunction reinstating his candidacy in an ongoing election. He has not met his burden to show that he is “indisputably” entitled to an injunction in his favor—under any of the claims he raises. And he asks this Court to 
take the extraordinary step to interfere with an ongoing election (which federal courts 
are loath to do, Purcell v. Gonzalez, 549 U.S. 1, 4–5 (2006)) by enjoining a minimally 
burdensome and duly-enacted State law that protects the integrity and fairness of 
elections, Burdick v. Takushi, 504 U.S. 428, 439–440 (1992), and the associational

2
rights of political parties, see Washington State Grange v. Washington State Republican Party, 552 U.S. 442, 459 (2008) (Roberts, C.J., concurring). 
Worse, Ronan asks this Court to circumvent any standards at all, much less the 
very high one for injunctions pending appeal, and to enter an interim injunction—
fashioned as an administrative stay. Having been refused an injunction twice below, 
Ronan cannot ask for a stay to obtain what he wants—placement on the ballot. 
This Court should reject both overreaching requests.
STATEMENT
1. In 2016, Plaintiff-Applicant Samuel Ronan, a member of the Democratic Party,
ran unopposed in the Democratic primary for the 62nd District of the Ohio House of 
Representatives. App.39–40, 44. He lost in the general election by a wide margin. 
See N.Y. Times, Ohio State House District 62: 2016 Election Results (2016),
https://perma.cc/84Y8-RRRZ.
Disillusioned by his loss in a deeply red district, Ronan changed tack: he would 
run as a Republican to make deep-red districts competitive for Democrats like himself. See App.213. In 2017, he ran for chair of the Democratic National Committee. 
App.45. On this national stage, Ronan continued to advocate for his strategy of running Democrats as Republicans in deeply red districts. App.61. He eventually withdrew his candidacy. See Domenico Montanaro & Scott Detrow, Perez Elected as 
Chairman of Democratic National Committee, NPR (Feb. 25, 2017), 
https://perma.cc/E5B9-K636. 
But he remained committed to his mission—hiding Democrats in Republican elections. He declared, “I put my money where my mouth is.” App.203 (quotation

3
omitted). And that he wanted to “put[] the rubber to the road” by employing the 
strategy himself. Id. (quotation omitted). So, in 2018, Ronan ran in the Republican 
primary for Ohio’s 1st Congressional District. App.202. According to Ronan, this was 
“the only way” he was “going to make it through” to voters in the 1st District. App.203
(quotation omitted). He was defeated in the primary election. See N.Y. Times, Ohio 
Primary Elections Results (May 8, 2018), https://perma.cc/G7ZN-BP2A.
After dabbling in a few other unsuccessful political campaigns—including, Ronan 
claims, as a self-described “dark horse protest” candidate in the 2024 Republican 
presidential primary, App.26–27, 46—Ronan turned to the instant election, the 2026 
midterms. He decided to run in the Republican primary in Ohio’s 15th Congressional 
District in July of 2025. App.46. He began collecting signatures in October 2025. 
App.47, 218. As part of that process, Ronan completed a “Declaration of Candidacy,” 
as required by Ohio Revised Code §3513.07. That statute requires candidates to sign 
a declaration stating: “I am a member of the ____ Party,” and “I further declare that, 
if elected to said office or position, I will qualify therefor, and that I will support and 
abide by the principles enunciated by the ____ Party.” Ohio Rev. Code §3513.07. 
Falsifying the election-candidacy declaration is a felony of the Fifth Degree. Id. As 
required by Ohio law, Ronan declared that he was “a member of the Republican 
Party” and if elected he would “support and abide by the principles enunciated by the 
Republican Party.” App.218.
But even after signing this form, Ronan continued to push his vision that Democrats like himself should primary Republicans in deep red districts to “get a foot in

4
the door.” App.217. In one notable exchange on social media, he was asked why he 
was running as a Republican despite having run for DNC chair just a few years back. 
App.217. In response, Ronan reiterated that he “very clearly mentioned in that very 
same DNC Chair race that Democrats, if they wanted to govern and regain the trust 
of Americans, would have to primary Republicans in deep red districts, as Republicans.” App.217. If “anything,” he continued, he was “following the argument” that 
he made on that stage by running as a Republican in a deep red primary. App.217. 
And he distanced himself from the Democratic Party, claiming he was “NOT fighting 
on behalf of the traitorous Democrats.” App.217. He was “running for office in the 
party of the dominant district.” App.217. In another social-media post in January 
2026, Ronan explained that “Leftists need to infiltrate republican spaces and primary 
them.” Samuel Ronan, Facebook (Jan. 15, 2026), https://www.facebook.com/groups/662717436755426/posts/881656498194851/?comment_id=890386273988540. He continued, “Which is why I said Democrats needed 
to primary republicans in red states as republicans when I ran for DNC Chair and 
why I am running as a Repuboican [sic] now...” Id. 
The Franklin County Board of Elections certified him as a candidate in February 
of this year. Ana Cordero (Ronan’s campaign manager and the other Plaintiff-Applicant in this case) posted a celebratory message on her personal social-media account. 
App.232–33. In response, someone said, “I’ve always wondered if it might be easier 
to torpedo the republican party from within as opposed to trying to take on the dems.”
App.233. Cordero responded, “yup! And we’re testing out [that] theory lol.” Id.

5
2. Marc A. Schare, a voter, filed a protest of Ronan’s candidacy. App.212–216. 
He alleged that there was clear and convincing evidence that Ronan “is not in fact a 
Republican.” App.212. Schare argued Ronan “has a long history of publicly denouncing the Republican party, its elected leaders, and its fundamental principles.” 
App.212. He alleged that Ronan was “pretending to be a Republican as a tool to get 
a foot in the door.” App.212 (quotation omitted). Schare further explained that this 
was “precisely the type of ‘opportunistic’ maneuvering the primary rules are designed 
to prevent.” Id. (quotation omitted). And he argued that Ronan’s declaration that 
he would “support and abide by the principles enunciated by the Republican Party” 
was “false,” and thus Ronan should be disqualified from appearing on the primary 
ballot. Id.
3. The Board of Elections held a hearing on Schare’s protest. Schare argued that 
Ronan’s Republican affiliation was a sham. Ronan argued that only voters could conduct a good-faith test of ideology, not the Board. App.342–43. The Board ultimately 
split, voting two-to-two on the protest. App.345–46. 
The issue was then referred to Ohio’s Secretary of State, Frank LaRose, App.346; 
see also Ohio Rev. Code §3501.11(X), who broke the tie in favor of Schare’s protest.
App.178–180. The Secretary explained that Ronan’s “public statements” made clear 
that Ronan was seeking the Republican nomination as part of his “longstanding strategy to have Democrats run as Republicans in Republican primaries.” App.179. He 
clarified that “the issue” was not about “ideological purity” but about “the integrity of 
the electoral process.” App.179. He noted that Ronan had “‘openly and repeatedly’

6
stated that he (and others) should run as Republicans, not because they are Republicans, but so that Democrats can get a foothold in Republican-leaning districts.” 
App.179. Those statements, even without applying any “ideological litmus test,” did 
“not show a change in affiliation but instead highlight[ed]” Ronan’s “ongoing mission 
to run Democrats as Republicans to infiltrate the party.” App.180. Last, he rebuffed 
Ronan’s contention that there is no “good faith” requirement for candidates seeking 
to affiliate with and run on the ballot of a political party. App.180.
4. Ronan and his campaign manager Coredero (together, “Ronan”) filed suit 
against LaRose and members of the Franklin County Board of Elections alleging violations of his rights under the First Amendment and the Elections Clause of the 
United States Constitution. And he alleged that Meredith Freehoff, a Board Member, 
violated his due-process rights by failing to recuse herself from the protest hearing 
before the Board because of an alleged conflict. App.2–3. At the outset, the district 
court granted a Temporary Restraining Order. App.3. After a hearing, the court 
denied a preliminary injunction, finding that his claims were unlikely to succeed because Ohio law’s good-faith requirement for candidacy was constitutional. Id. The 
court stayed its ruling and extended the TRO to noon on April, 6, 2026 to allow the 
Sixth Circuit to weigh in on a forthcoming request for stay pending appeal (though 
fashioned as a stay pending appeal, the request for preliminary relief in that posture 
is correctly categorized as an injunction pending appeal). Id.
5. The Sixth Circuit rejected Ronan’s request for an injunction pending appeal. 
App.1–2. It agreed that Ronan is unlikely to show that Ohio’s good-faith requirement

7
violated the First Amendment. App.4–6. Applying Anderson-Burdick balancing, the 
court noted that the good-faith requirement was not a severe burden on Ronan’s candidacy because it “does not prevent Ronan from voting, supporting candidates, endorsing candidates, running for office, or even switching parties.” App.5. Truthfulness in candidacy was not any severe burden. The court noted that the State had a 
substantial interest in protecting the fairness and integrity of elections, preventing 
fraud and corrupt practices, and avoiding confusion. App.6. And the good-faith measure was a reasonable means to achieve these interests. All in, Ohio’s good-faith requirement likely passed constitutional muster. Last, the court quickly dismissed the 
Elections Clause and due-process claims. App.6–7. 
Because the First Amendment is implicated in this case, the first factor in an injunction-pending-appeal analysis—the likelihood of success on the merits—is largely 
dispositive. See App.3–4. The Sixth Circuit denied the motion in full. The district 
court’s TRO expired on April 6, at noon. See App.3. Early voting began on Tuesday 
April 7, 2026 in Ohio. Ohio Sec’y of State, 2026 Voting Schedule (Text Only),
https://perma.cc/48MR-Q8PC. 
STANDARD OF REVIEW
An injunction pending appeal is “extraordinary relief.” Hobby Lobby Stores, Inc. 
v. Sebelius, 568 U.S. 1401, 1403 (2012) (Sotomayor, J., in chambers). To obtain an 
injunction in this posture, the applicant must demonstrate that “the legal rights at 
issue are ‘indisputably clear.’” Lux v. Rodrigues, 561 U.S. 1306, 1307 (2010) (Roberts, 
C.J., in chambers) (quoting Turner Broadcasting System, Inc. v. FCC, 507 U.S. 1301,

8
1303 (1993) (Rehnquist, C. J., in chambers)). That is because such injunctions “do[]
not simply suspend judicial alteration of the status quo but grant[] judicial intervention that has been withheld by lower courts” and therefore “demand[] a significantly 
higher justification” than that required for a stay. Ohio Citizens for Responsible Energy, Inc. v. NRC, 479 U.S. 1312, 1312 (1986) (Scalia, J., in chambers).
“A plaintiff seeking a preliminary injunction must establish that he is likely to 
succeed on the merits, that he is likely to suffer irreparable harm in the absence of 
preliminary relief, that the balance of equities tips in his favor, and that an injunction 
is in the public interest.” Winter v. Nat. Res. Def. Council, Inc., 555 U.S. 7, 20 (2008). 
The last two considerations merge when the movant seeks to enjoin the government. 
Nken v. Holder, 556 U.S. 418, 435 (2009). 
Applicants, like Ronan, seeking injunctions pending appeal face additional hurdles. First, they must show that this Court would likely grant certiorari on the questions presented. See Hollingsworth v. Perry, 558 U.S. 183, 190 (2010) (per curiam); 
Labrador v. Poe, 144 S. Ct. 921, 931 (2024) (Kavanaugh, J., concurring); Does 1-3 v. 
Mills, 142 S. Ct. 17, 18 (2021) (Barrett, J., concurring). Second, the “traditional test 
for a stay or [injunction]” applies differently “in election cases” where a plaintiff seeks 
to enjoin “a state’s election laws in the period close to an election.” Merrill v. Milligan, 
142 S. Ct. 879, 880 (Mem.) (2022) (Kavanaugh, J., concurring); see id. (collecting 
cases). “[F]ederal courts” ordinarily refrain from “alter[ing] the election rules on the 
eve of an election.” Abbott v. League of United Latin American Citizens, 146 S. Ct. 
418, 419 (2025); (quoting Republican National Committee v. Democratic National

9
Committee, 589 U.S. 423, 424 (2020) (per curiam)); Purcell v. Gonzalez, 549 U.S. 1, 4–
5 (2006). Such interference—especially where, as here, the election is already underway—causes “chaos and confusion.” Merrill, 142 S. Ct. at 880 (Kavanaugh, J., concurring). All told, a request to enjoin a state law in the middle of an ongoing election 
after two lower courts have refused that relief faces an all-but-insurmountable obstacle. Only a glaring constitutional violation could justify the relief sought here. 
Ronan additionally requests an “administrative stay” that places him back on the 
ballot. That is a mislabeling. Because Ronan lost on his motion for a preliminary 
injunction, and for a stay of the district court’s order pending appeal (properly characterized as a renewed request for an injunction pending appeal), the parties sit in 
status quo ante. Any order putting him on the ballot now is an injunction, not a stay. 
With that reorientation in mind, a request to pause proceedings before this Court 
applies the very high standards for injunctive relief is essentially a request for a 
standardless injunction. See United States v. Texas, 144 S. Ct. 797, 798 (2024) (Barrett, J., concurring). The threshold for receiving one should exceed even the highest 
standards articulated by this Court. 
ARGUMENT
I. Ronan is unlikely to succeed on the merits.
A. Ronan cannot succeed on his First Amendment Claim.
1. The First Amendment does not restrict the State from promoting order, fairness, and integrity in their elections. Nor does it stop the State from facilitating 
political parties’ associational rights under the First Amendment. Take each in turn.

10
The First Amendment places some limits on state ballot-access laws, but not in 
the way Ronan’s Application envisions. The Court explained decades ago that the 
First Amendment writes no blank check for candidates to appear on a ballot, even 
though it does prevent States from enacting full-on prohibitions against, for example, 
independent candidates. See, e.g., Burdick v. Takushi, 504 U.S. 428 (1992); Williams 
v. Rhodes, 393 U.S. 23 (1968). The First Amendment’s role in ballot access is not a 
one-to-one correspondence with the First Amendment’s guarantees in political speech 
generally. Instead, “[a]ttributing to elections a more generalized expressive function 
would undermine the ability of States to operate elections fairly and efficiently.” Burdick, 504 U.S. at 439. The First Amendment, that is, recognizes that the States “may, 
and inevitably must, enact reasonable regulations of parties, elections, and ballots to 
reduce election- and campaign-related disorder.” Timmons v. Twin Cities Area New 
Party, 520 U.S. 351, 358 (1997).
When it comes to state regulation of parties and ballots, this Court’s cases repeatedly recognize that the First Amendment leaves States wide latitude to regulate 
party primaries and other candidate-selection mechanics so that those processes are 
characterized more by order than disorder. To promote order, and “the integrity of 
the various routes to the ballot,” Storer v. Brown, 415 U.S. 724, 733 (1974), States 
may, for example, require independent candidates to demonstrate sufficient voter 
support to appear on the ballot, may ban write-in candidates, and may 
prohibit candidates who secure the endorsement of two parties from appearing on the

11
ballot under the banner of both parties, see Jenness v. Fortson, 403 U.S. 431, 442 
(1971); Burdick, 504 U.S. at 439; Timmons 520 U.S. at 354. 
The Court has also recognized the States’ power to promote orderly elections by 
regulating who can run and vote in party primaries. On the candidate side, a State 
can ban a candidate from a partisan primary-election ballot if the candidate had been 
registered with any other political party in the year leading up to declaring candidacy 
for the partisan primary. Storer, 415 U.S. at 733. On the voter side, States may 
require primary-election voters to have been registered with the relevant party ahead 
of the election. Rosario v. Rockefeller, 410 U.S. 752, 753, 762 (1973). A state may 
even prohibit a political party from inviting voters registered with other parties from 
voting in its primary. Clingman v. Beaver, 544 U.S. 581, 587 (2005). The Court has 
even upheld a political party’s requirement that its candidates pledge to support the 
winner of a nominating convention. Although that was not a First Amendment decision, the Court detected “no federal constitutional objection” to the pledge mandate. 
Ray v. Blair, 343 U.S. 214, 231 (1952).
There are, though, limits on States’ power to regulate primary voting and primary 
candidates. Those limits follow from the general associational rights the First 
Amendment protects. Those rights run in both directions. In one direction, States 
do not have unchecked latitude to block a political party from allowing independent 
voters to participate in its primaries. Tashjian v. Republican Party of Conn., 479 U.S. 
208, 225 (1986). In the other direction, States may not force a political party to open 
its primary to all voters. California Democratic Party v. Jones, 530 U.S. 567, 577

12
(2000). Jones recognizes that “a corollary of the right to associate is the right not to 
associate.” Id. at 574; see also, e.g., Boy Scouts of Am. v. Dale, 530 U.S. 640 (2000); 
Hurley v. Irish–American Gay, Lesbian and Bisexual Group of Boston, 515 U.S. 557 
(1995); cf. Hosanna-Tabor Evangelical Lutheran Church & Sch. v. E.E.O.C., 565 U.S. 
171, 196 (2012). 
In short, while the States have significant power to regulate candidates and voters 
in primary elections, they may not “force[] political parties to associate with … those 
who … have expressly affiliated with a rival,” Jones, 530 U.S. at 581, or “force parties 
to accept candidates they do not want,” Washington State Grange v. Washington 
State Republican Party, 552 U.S. 442, 459 (2008) (Roberts, C.J., concurring).
2. Ohio’s good-faith requirement for candidate declarations respects political parties’ associational rights by shielding parties from candidates who do not share their 
values. Conditioning ballot access on a candidate’s affirmation that the candidate is 
“a member of” the party and “will support and abide by the principles of” the party, 
Ohio Rev. Code §3513.07, is a logical way to promote order and confidence in primary 
elections. Ohio’s law thus easily satisfies the Court’s oft-deployed “balancing test” for 
voting regulations that weighs the burden on voting against the governmental interest in running orderly elections that engender voter confidence. Crawford v. Marion 
Cnty. Election Bd., 553 U.S. 181, 190, 195–200 (2008) (Stevens, J., Op.). Indeed, 
Ohio’s “effort to respect” political parties’ “First Amendment interests,” WilliamsYulee v. Fla. Bar, 575 U.S. 433, 451 (2015), should leave little doubt that it survives 
any First Amendment scrutiny.

13
3. Ronan pushes back on the good-faith requirement’s constitutional bonafides by 
drawing on three cases, but each is woefully inadequate for the task. Ronan first 
spends pages detailing the litigation (including a decision from this Court) about 
Ohio’s former law regulating campaign speech. Ronan Appl.15–17. Those decisions 
about candidates’ campaign speeches hold little to no relevance in this case about 
ballot access. As the above discussion shows, States have far more power to regulate 
ballot access than campaign speech. Indeed, equating the two “would undermine the 
ability of States to operate elections fairly and efficiently.” Burdick, 504 U.S. at 439. 
Ronan also cites cases about viewpoint discrimination as justifying his request for 
an emergency injunction. Ronan Appl.17 (citing, e.g., Miami Herald Pub. Co. v. 
Tornillo, 418 U.S. 241 (1974)). Again, the comparison is inapt. Whatever the evils of 
such discrimination for speech generally, those cases do not govern in the context of 
political-party association. If they did, the Court would not have held that California 
could not force political parties to accept all voters in partisan primaries or held that 
Oklahoma could ban non-party voters from partisan primaries. See Jones, 530 U.S.
at 577; Clingman, 544 U.S. at 588.
Finally, and puzzlingly, Ronan cites Dale, a case upholding an associational right 
of exclusion. Ronan Appl.18. In Ronan’s view, Dale means that courts cannot secondguess private entities’ associational choices. But Ohio law facilitates those rights by 
requiring candidates to affirm that they have honestly declared party membership 
and commitment to that political party’s “principles.” Ohio Rev. Code §3513.07.

14
At bottom, Ronan’s request is upside down. Political parties possess a First 
Amendment associational right to exclude those who do not share their values. So it 
would be quite surprising if the First Amendment forbids States from protecting that 
right when the Amendment “barely—and only provisionally—permits” States to compel association. See Schuette v. Coal. to Defend Affirmative Action, Integration & Immigrant Rts. & Fight for Equal. By Any Means Necessary (BAMN), 572 U.S. 291, 317 
(2014) (Scalia, J., concurring in the judgment). Dale itself is a leading case about the 
associational right not to “accept members where such acceptance would derogate 
from the organization’s expressive message.” 530 U.S. at 661. 
At the very least, in this posture, Ronan’s right to an injunction is not “indisputably clear.” Lux, 561 U.S. at 1307 (quotation omitted).
B. Ronan has failed to state a claim under the Elections Clause and 
even if he did, he cannot succeed on it.
Ronan next asserts that his removal from the ballot violates the Elections Clause. 
Fatal to his claim, he does not explain how his removal violated that clause. His bare 
arguments include that he has standing and a §1983 cause of action to challenge his 
removal under that clause. See Ronan Appl.18–20. Even assuming he is right, standing and a cause of action do not entitle him to an injunction. He must show that he 
is likely to succeed on the merits of his Elections Clause claim to be entitled to an 
injunction. He has not even tried.
Even if he had tried, he would have failed. That is because his Elections Clause 
claim would add nothing to his First Amendment claim. Cf., e.g., Burdick, 504 U.S.

15
at 433–34; Timmons, 520 U.S. at 357–58. If there exists an Elections Clause argument that is distinct from his First Amendment argument, Ronan does not make it.
C. Ronan cannot succeed on his due-process claim.
Ronan’s federal due-process claim is likewise unlikely to succeed. His argument 
is as follows: a Board Member, Freedhoff, who voted to remove Ronan from the ballot
for violating Ohio’s good-faith requirement, served as vice-chair in the Ohio Republican Party, which had endorsed and financially supported (through its subsidiary, the 
Franklin County Republican Party) Ronan’s opponent. Ronan Appl.5–6, 14, 20. So, 
he argues, she should have been disqualified from participating in the hearing because she was “personally financially interested” in the outcome. Ronan Appl.20. 
This does not suffice to obtain an extraordinary injunction pending appeal for two 
reasons.
First, this Court has said that candidates for political office do not have a property 
or liberty interest in an elected position. Snowden v. Hughes, 321 U.S. 1, 7 (1944). 
So even if Ronan was wrongly denied a right to political office, any claim arising from 
that denial cannot be “secured” under the Due Process Clause. Id. But Ronan claims 
a circuit split. Ronan Appl.20–21 (collecting cases). Maybe so, but that counsels 
against relief because when the circuits are split on the critical issue of whether a 
due-process right even exists, Ronan’s right to relief is anything but “indisputably 
clear.” Lux, 561 U.S. at 1307–08 (explaining that circuit divergence on the legal issue 
defeats the “indisputably clear” standard for injunctive relief).
Second, even if Ronan had asserted a viable due-process claim, it fails on its merits. As the Sixth Circuit noted, Ronan conceded that he had “no evidence of any

16
personal financial benefit to Freedhoff” or that she had discussed the protest hearing 
with the Ohio Republican Party. App.7. And he offers nothing now beyond mere 
speculation and vague, attenuated theories of how Freedhoff could have potentially 
been influenced by her connection to the Ohio Republican Party and its potential connections. Ronan Appl.22. Nothing rises to the “probability of actual bias” that “is too 
high to be constitutionally tolerable.” Caperton v. A. T. Massey Coal Co., 556 U.S. 
868, 872 (2009) (quotation omitted). 
II. The remaining equities weigh against enjoining a duly-enacted State 
law, this Court is unlikely to grant certiorari, and this Court should 
not enter the election fray when Ronan has not shown he is 
indisputably entitled to an injunction.
Because Ronan seeks an injunction to vindicate his constitutional rights, this case 
largely ends where Ronan’s likelihood of success on the merits fails. Nevertheless, 
the balance of equities and the public interest, which merge in this case, undermine 
Ronan’s extraordinary request for a first-in-time injunction from this Court. Nken, 
556 U.S. at 435. For one thing, “[a]ny time a State is enjoined by a court from effectuating statutes enacted by representatives of its people, it suffers a form of irreparable injury.” Trump v. CASA, 606 U.S. 831, 861 (2025) (quoting Maryland v. King, 
567 U.S. 1301, 1303 (2012) (Roberts, C.J., in chambers) (additional quotation marks 
omitted)). That means it is the State that will be injured by an injunction from this 
Court. That is especially true here because the State retains the power to regulate 
its own election. Burdick, 504 U.S. at 433. And it has an overwhelming interest in 
protecting the fairness and integrity of its elections by protecting against sham

17
candidacies, party raiding, and voter confusion. See id. at 439–40. All this is truer
now because the election is already underway. Purcell v. Gonzalez, 549 U.S. 1, 4–5 
(2006).
Ronan cannot clear the two other procedural hurdles required of applicants seeking an injunction pending appeal: certworthiness and an indisputable legal entitlement to an injunction. See Hollingsworth, 558 U.S. at 190; Lux, 561 U.S. at 1307. 
On certworthiness, this Court is unlikely to grant certiorari in this case. Only the 
due-process claim features a circuit split—that too, a lopsided one against Ronan’s 
position. Even if the Court wanted to resolve that split, this case would not be the 
preferred vehicle to do so. And the remaining claims concern only straightforward 
applications of this Court’s well-established law. A certworthy question is nowhere 
to be seen. On indisputable legal entitlement, for the reasons discussed above, Ronan 
has not shown that he is indisputably entitled to an injunction. Above 9–16. 
That means this Court should hesitate to interfere with an election that is already 
underway. Putting Ronan on the ballot now given how unlikely he is to ultimately 
prevail in this litigation will cause “chaos and confusion.” Merrill, 142 S. Ct. at 880 
(Mem.) (Kavanaugh, J., concurring). “[E]ven heroic efforts” by state officials “likely 
would not be enough to avoid” the turmoil that will follow. Id.

18
CONCLUSION
The Court should deny the requests for injunction pending appeal, administrative 
stay, and expedited briefing.
April 2026 Respectfully submitted,

Dear Chairman Preisse and Board Members, 
I have reviewed the tie vote referred to me by the Franklin County Board of Elections
(“the Board”) on March 13, 2026, as well as the arguments, authorities, and evidence 
submitted to my office. I now break the tie vote submitted to my office in favor of the
protest against the candidacy of Samuel Ronan for Representative from the 15th
Congressional District. 
Background Information 
A protest was timely filed with the Franklin County Board of Elections regarding the
candidacy of Samual Ronan as a Republican candidate for the office of Representative 
to Congress from the 15th District. On March 6, 2026, the Board met and held a hearing
on the protest. The protest, which was brought by Marc A. Schare, alleged that Mr.
Ronan is not a Republican and therefore should not be on the May 5, 2026, primary
ballot as a candidate for Congress. 
At the conclusion of the hearing, and following a closed session to deliberate, board
member Jamie Shumaker made the following motion: 
After conducting a hearing regarding the protest against the candidacy of Samuel Ronan, 
a Republican candidate for Representative to Congress in the 15th District, submitted by 
Marc Schare…I move that the Franklin County Board of Elections determine that the
candidate’s declaration of candidacy and petition of Samual Ronan are valid and deny the
protest based on the evidence presented at this hearing. I find that the protest [sic] failed

The motion was seconded by Member Michael Sexton. 
The Board vote resulted in a tie. Members Shumaker and Sexton voted to deny the
protest, and Chairman Preisse and Member Freedhoff voted in favor of the protest. 
On March 13, 2026, the Board submitted this tie vote to me for consideration in
accordance with Ohio Revised Code Section 3501.11(X). On that date, the Board also

the hearing, and a copy of the hearing transcript. Additionally, although not consistent
with established practice, counsel for the candidate and counsel for the protester each

Analysis 
After consideration of the arguments and the materials provided, I am breaking the tie
in favor of the protest. Mr. Ronan’s public statements, and those of individuals 
associated with him and his candidacy, make clear that Mr. Ronan is seeking the
Republican nomination as part of his longstanding strategy to have Democrats run as
Republicans in Republican primaries. 
As Board Members Preisse and Freedhoff argued in their letter explaining their vote, the
issue here is not “ideological purity.” Members of political parties are obviously free to
disagree internally about a range of issues, and my decision does not suggest otherwise. 
However, this case presents questions about the integrity of the electoral process. As 
Members Preisse and Freedhoff point out, Mr. Ronan has “openly and repeatedly”
stated that he (and others) should run as Republicans, not because they are Republicans,
but so that Democrats can get a foothold in Republican-leaning districts. The goal of his
scheme is to get voters to vote for Democrats, believing they are voting for Republicans.

my office. Mr. Ronan’s merit brief included arguments and allegations that Board Member
Freedhoff had a conflict of interest and was required to abstain from participating in Mr. Ronan’s
hearing. I find these arguments without merit. It is worth noting that the two Democratic board
members did not mention the alleged conflict of interest in their statements supporting their

Mr. Ronan argues that there is no “good faith” requirement on candidates seeking to
affiliate with political parties in order to run for office. I agree that it is not the job of the
state or this office to impose ideological litmus tests on a candidate’s self-identification. 
But again, that is not the fact pattern presented here. 
On each petition, Mr. Ronan declared that if elected, he would support and abide by the
principles enunciated by the Republican Party. He signed this declaration. Yet there is
ample evidence demonstrating that his goal is not to support the party’s principles, but
rather for Democrats to “primary Republicans…just to get a foot in the door.” (Exhibit 
P2). To be clear, candidates can change party affiliation. (See R.C. 3513.191). Here, 
however, Mr. Ronan’s statements do not show a change in affiliation but instead
highlight his ongoing mission to run Democrats as Republicans to infiltrate the party. 
I reject Mr. Ronan’s apparent argument that a candidate may affiliate with a political
party in bad faith. In another context—specifically, the question of whether a candidate
has disaffiliated from a political party in order to become an “independent”—both state
and federal courts have required that the candidate’s action be undertaken in good
faith. See State ex rel. Coughlin v. Summit Cty. Bd of Elections, 136 Ohio St.3d 371, 375
(2013) (citing Morrison v. Colley, 467 F.3d 503, 509 (6th Cir. 2006)); Jolivette v. Husted, 
886 F. Supp.2d 820, 823-24, 833 (S.D. Ohio Aug. 15, 2012). Those cases are instructive 
here. 
For the foregoing reasons, I break the tie in favor of the protest and against certifying 
Mr. Ronan to the May 5, 2026, Republican Primary Election Ballot for the Representative 
to Congress for the 15th District.

On February 20, 2026, a protest against Mr. Ronan's candidacy was filed by Marc A. Schare, a member 
of the Republican Party and a qualified elector in the State of Ohio. In part, Mr. Schare contends: 
"Ronan has a long history of publicly denouncing the Republican party, its elected leaders, and its

- Schare Protest, p.1 
Mr. Schare further states:

affiliation." 
- Schare Protest, p.4 
An administrative hearing was conducted on March 6, 2026 to review the relevant facts related to Mr. 
Schare' s protest. 
Legal Analysis 
Based on a review of the applicable legal standards, including R.C. 3513.191, and published guidance 
from the Ohio Secretary of State, we believe that Mr. Ronan should remain on the ballot. 
R.C. 3513.191 sets forth the party-affiliation requirements for candidates in party primary elections, which 
may form the basis of a challenge under R.C. 3513.05. The relevant language provides: 
R.C. 3513.19l(A): 
"No person shall be a candidate for nomination or election at a party primary if the person voted as a 
member of a different political party at any primary election within the current year and the immediately 
preceding two calendar years." 
However, R.C. 3513.191(8) provides an important exception: 
"Notwithstanding division (A) of this section, either of the following persons may be candidates for 
nomination of any political party at a party primary: 
( 1) A person who does not hold an elective office; 
(2) A person who holds an elective office other than one for which candidates are nominated at a party 
primary." 
This same provision is reiterated in the Ohio Secretary of State's 2026 Ohio Candidate Requirement 
Guide, which states: 
"A person may be a candidate for nomination of any political party at a primary election (regardless of 
party affiliation established by voting in a prior partisan primary) if either of the following apply (R.C. 
3513.191):

relative to the protest of the candidacy of Mr. Samuel Peter Ronan, on 3/6/2026, regarding his putative

The issue raised at the hearing was not ideological purity. From our perspective, it was about preserving 
the integrity of the primary process. Mr. Ronan has openly and repeatedly admitted he was running as a 
Republican because it was the only way that Democrats could get a foothold in a Republican district. 
He declared this when he was running for chairman of the Democratic National Committee, no less, 
and again on social media, an example of which was included as part of the formal protest. Much the 
same was also stated during the podcast interview that was submitted and played at the hearing. Our 
conclusion that Mr. Ronan should not remain on the ballot as a Republican is based on his own past, 
recent, and repeated declarations. 
Mr. Brown, Ronan's attorney, stated that Ohio law does not prohibit bad faith when one signs a 
declaration of candidacy. If he is adjudicated correct, one could assert that the right strategy for the 
Franklin County Republican Party and, indeed, the Ohio Republican Party, is to run Republicans in 
every Democratic district in Franklin County and, indeed, the State of Ohio. Mr. Ronan made the point 
that people will not consider his views in a Republican district so he has to masquerade, thinly veiled, 
and run as a Republican. That view, if carried to its logical conclusion, would negate any benefit or 
rationale for party primaries. Republicans can then run in Democratic districts as 
Democrats, and we would anticipate 
Democrats would continue to follow Mr. Ronan's strategy and do the same in Republican 
districts. Mr. Ronan is the test case that, should he be approved to run as a Republican, would set a 
dangerous precedent. 
Mr. Ronan signed a sworn partisan declaration. But it is abundantly clear he misrepresented himself. He 
stated he is "gaming the system". He presented no evidence that he has met with the Franklin County

V. The Federal Constitution Prohibits States from Placing Political Ideological 
Requirements on Congressional Candidates.
Candidates within a political party can and do disagree over their party’s proper 
principles. Indeed, they must. That is what builds the party’s evolving platform and establishes 
the “principles enunciated by the Republican Party.” Mr. Ronan can be a member of the 
Republican party without agreeing with each and every Republican about anything and 
everything. He can truthfully declare that he will support and abide by party principles in the 
future, whatever they may turn out to be in Ohio following the primaries, even though others in 
the party disagree. It is up to Republican voters – and not a single protestor or this Board of 
Elections -- to choose their party’s principles and the candidates who will best support them. To 
the extent the protestor is correct, and Ohio law allows a board of elections to remove a 
candidate for not being Republican enough, not being a good faith Republican, or not truthfully 
stating a future intent to abide by undefined and unknowable “party principles,” that 
interpretation of Ohio law would violate both the Elections Clause in Article I of the United 
States Constitution and the Constitution’s First Amendment.
The Supreme Court of the United States observed in Cook v. Gralike, 531 U.S. 510 
(2001), that unlike local and State elections, State ballot restrictions on congressional (House and 
Senate) races are governed not by powers found in State Constitutions but by the grant of 
authority to States located in section 4 of Article I of the United States Constitution. This federal 
grant of power allows States to “regulate the ‘Times, Places and Manner of holding Elections for 
Senators and Representatives,’ subject to a grant of authority to Congress to ‘make or alter such 
Regulations.’” Id. at 522 (quoting U.S. Const., art.I, § 4). “No other constitutional provision 
gives the States authority over congressional elections, and no such authority could be reserved 
under the Tenth Amendment.” Id. at 522-23. 
The Court further explained that while States have authority to enact “procedural 
regulations,” id. at 523, they have no “power to dictate electoral outcomes, to favor or disfavor a 
class of candidates, or to evade important constitutional restraints.” Id. (citation omitted). 
Applying this logic to Missouri’s attempt to force candidates to include labels on their ballots 
stating whether they supported term limits, the Court had little difficulty concluding that the 
federal Elections Clause had been violated. “[Missouri’s law] is not a procedural regulation. It 
does not regulate the time of elections; it does not regulate the place of elections; nor, we believe, 
does it regulate the manner of elections.” Id. (footnote omitted). It “bears no relation to the 
‘manner’ of elections as we understand it ….” Id. “Rather, [it] is plainly designed to favor 
candidates who are willing to support the particular form of a term limits amendment set forth in 
its text and to disfavor those who either oppose term limits entirely or would prefer a different 
proposal.” Id. (emphasis added) “[F]ar from regulating the procedural mechanisms of elections, 
it attempts to ‘dictate electoral outcomes.’ Such ‘regulation’ of congressional elections simply is 
not authorized by the Elections Clause.” Id. at 525-26 (citation omitted and emphasis added).
Justice Kennedy joined in the Court’s unanimous decision, adding that “[a] State is not 
permitted to interpose itself between the people and their National Government as it seeks to do 
here.” Id. at 527 (Kennedy, J., concurring) (emphasis added). “In today's case the question is not 
close. Here the State attempts to intrude upon the relationship between the people and their 
congressional delegates by seeking to control or confine the discretion of those delegates, and the 
interference is not permissible.” Id. at 530 (emphasis added).

Limiting party primary ballots to those candidates who are genuine members of that party serves 
the state's legitimate interests in "avoiding overcrowded ballots'' and "protect[ing] the integrity of 
its political processes from frivolous or fraudulent candidacies.'' Jolivette, 694 F.3d at 769 quoting 
Bullock v. Carter, 405 U.S. 134, 145 ( 1972). Moreover, "the state has an interest in regulating 
ballot access in order to avoid confusion, deception, and even ftustration of the democratic process 
at the general election. Id. (internal quotation marks and citations omitted).

undermine these important objectives and undermine the integrity of Ohio's primary system.

(e) Review By the Witness; Changes.
(1) Review; Statement of Changes. On request by the 
deponent or a party before the deposition is
completed, the deponent must be allowed 30 days 
after being notified by the officer that the
transcript or recording is available in which:
(A) to review the transcript or recording; and
(B) if there are changes in form or substance, to 
sign a statement listing the changes and the
reasons for making them.
(2) Changes Indicated in the Officer's Certificate.
The officer must note in the certificate prescribed 
by Rule 30(f)(1) whether a review was requested
and, if so, must attach any changes the deponent 
makes during the 30-day period.
